props.title: The India Reality
props.sub: The rulebook, and the honest numbers

captions: Part three.
The India reality.
A bot doesn't run in a vacuum — it
runs inside a broker and an exchange rulebook.
Think of a driving licence and a number plate
— for your bot.
The rulebook has dates, a speed cap, an identity,
and controls.
Here are the pieces. S E B I issued

the framework on the fourth of February twenty
twenty-five,
and it applies to all brokers from the first
of April twenty twenty-six.
The example threshold: at or below ten orders per
second, an A P I algo gets a generic
Algo I D; above it, the algo must be
registered. Access needs a static I P and two-factor
login.

Plainly, every bot must be identified, rate-limited,
and supervised
— the broker is the principal.

Technically, that's the S E B I retail-algo
framework,
with an exchange kill switch and a five-year audit
trail.
Now the part that decides everything: costs.
Every trade leaks a little, like a slightly leaky
bucket.
On the chart, gross returns fall into smaller net
returns as trading picks up.

For example: securities-transaction tax of zero
point zero five
percent on futures, zero point one five percent on
options, plus about twenty rupees a broker order and
eighteen percent G S T — that's a Zerodha
example, not every broker.

Plainly, automation is not an edge; costs decide
whether
high turnover can survive.
The sobering technical fact: a S E B I

study found ninety-three percent of over one crore
individual

futures-and-options traders lost money across
financial years twenty twenty-two
to twenty-four — losses above one point eight lakh
crore rupees. That's F and O traders, not algo
users.
